list.listitem: A high index of suspicion for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) is warranted for patients with a foreign body sensation associated with hammering, grinding, or other force-related mechanism. C
Refer most, if not all, patients with IOFB urgently to an ophthalmologist. C
Following the diagnosis with an ocular examination and imaging, surgical intervention and accompanying antibiotics and steroids may be necessary for maximal visual recovery. C
Complications such as endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy may complicate rehabilitation. C
Even with devastating injuries, the modest chance for functional success dictates reconstruction efforts prior to enucleation. C
Safety glasses may prevent most cases of IOFB injury. C

background.definition: Intraocular foreign body (IOFB) is the presence of a foreign body in the eye from a penetrating injury.

list.listitem: There are 2.5 million eye injuries annually in the United States.
The lifetime prevalence of eye injury is 1400 per 100,000.
Job-related eye trauma, which is 20% of all eye injuries, costs $300 million annually in the United States.
Eighty-one percent of eye injuries are in men; median age 26 years, mean age 29 years.
Trauma is the leading cause of enucleation in children older than 3 years.
Ninety percent of all eye injuries are preventable.
The United States Eye Injury Registry estimates that 500,000 years of lost eyesight occur annually in the United States.
Globally, the total all-age prevalence and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) due to IOFBs rose by 41.9 and 35.5% from 1990 to 2021.
Trauma: young men are the most frequently affected.
Occupation-related: most commonly reported in construction workers.
Damage and final resting place depend on ocular penetration site and characteristics of IOFB, including size, shape, and velocity on impact.
The most commonly injured eye structures include the cornea, lens, and retina.
A posterior segment injury carries a risk of blindness twice that of anterior segment injury.
Eye morbidity results from the initial injury plus long-term risk of endophthalmitis, severe inflammation, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, retinal detachment, or retinal toxicity.
There is insufficient evidence from RCTs that educational interventions reduce eye injuries.C

Protective eyewear (polycarbonate safety glasses or goggles), especially in high-risk activities such as construction, paintball games, BB gun use, ball sports, may decrease the risk of ocular injury and IOFB. C

A high index of suspicion is needed with any ocular injury or ruptured globe, especially when a foreign body sensation is associated with a history of hammering, grinding, or other force-related mechanism. C
Careful slit lamp examination and dilated fundus examination are necessary. C
If the orbital globe is clearly ruptured, the remainder of the examination should be performed only in the operating room. C
Imaging with CT, MRI, plain film, or B-scan ultrasound may be helpful in uncertain situations, with MRI contraindicated if there is suspicion of metallic foreign body. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Presenting signs and symptoms often the same; key point is no IOFB
Hypopyon instead of hyphema, vitritis instead of vitreous hemorrhage
Consider occult IOFB, which can present with unilateral inflammation

list.listitem: Symptoms pertaining to a change in visual acuity and/or eye pain are variable and may not be present.

On examination, a corneal or scleral perforation site may be seen. Other examination findings that suggest a ruptured or open globe include low or elevated intraocular pressure; severe subconjunctival hemorrhage; deep or shallow anterior chamber; hyphema; irregular pupil; limitation of extraocular motility; a damaged, dislocated, or subluxed lens; and vitreous hemorrhage.
Additional slit lamp findings suggestive of IOFB include microcystic edema of peripheral cornea, iris transillumination defect, and anterior or posterior segment inflammation.
A long-standing iron IOFB can cause siderosis, anisocoria, heterochromia, corneal deposits, anterior subcapsular cataracts, lens dislocation, and optic atrophy.
The composition of the foreign body determines the severity of the inflammatory reaction. See .
Imaging alone cannot be relied on for a definite answer apart from the clinical examination and possible surgical exploration.

CT of the orbit and brain (axial and coronal, with 1 mm cuts through orbit) is the imaging study of choice. In cases of IOFBs with open globe injury, CT has been shown to be more effective than clinical eye exam or B-scan, irrespective of IOFB location. Plain film may be useful for a metallic foreign body if CT scan is unavailable. MRI may be superior for wood, glass, plastic, or organic material, but is contraindicated for metallic foreign body.
Consider ultrasound biomicroscopy for occult anterior foreign bodies. Consider B-scan ultrasound to help localize IOFB and rule out retinal tears or retinal detachment.
Consider culturing the wound site if it appears infected.
The likelihood of a penetrating injury is increased in patients presenting with a foreign body sensation associated with hammering, grinding, or other similar force-related mechanism.
The initial ocular examination should include use of the slit lamp before and (if indicated) after fundus dilation. Defer gonioscopy and scleral depression if globe integrity is in question.
If the globe is clearly ruptured, the remainder of the examination should be performed only in the operating room.
Emergent repair of the ruptured globe is indicated, with the timing of the removal of the IOFB dependent on the clinical scenario. C
Systemic as well as topical antibiotics and corticosteroids may help decrease the risk of endophthalmitis and decrease ocular inflammation. C
Primary wound closure or a self-sealing wound within 24 hours is associated with a lower risk of endophthalmitis. B
Intravitreal antibiotics can help decrease the risk of posttraumatic endophthalmitis in patients with IOFB. B
Despite lack of definitive evidence, systemic antibiotics (cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours and ciprofloxacin 400 mg orally or IV every 12 hours) are recommended in all cases of open globe.

Postoperative regimen typically consists of topical antibiotics (fortified drops vs fourth-generation quinolone), cycloplegic agent for comfort and to prevent scarring, and topical corticosteroids to help decrease intraocular inflammation.
For prophylaxis of acute posttraumatic bacterial endophthalmitis in cases with retained IOFB, intravitreal antibiotics are effective.

The use of topical anesthetics for associated simple corneal abrasions is typically not recommended, though some protocols describe their safety in short-term use (e.g., no more than 1.5 to 2 mL total of proparacaine, tetracaine, or oxybuprocaine up to every 30 minutes as needed within the first 24 hours after presentation).
Emergent repair is needed for a ruptured globe.
Timing of surgery to remove IOFB is controversial; it is uncertain whether emergent removal vs delayed removal decreases the risk for endophthalmitis.
Posterior hyaloid should be detached surgically, and any impact site treated prophylactically.
Posterior chamber IOFB generally requires pars plana vitrectomy, whereas anterior chamber IOFB can be removed by secondary limbal incision.
A magnet may be useful for the removal of a metallic foreign body.
Endophthalmitis is associated with foreign bodies in up to 13.5% of cases.
Long-standing IOFB may require removal if it is visually significant or if severe inflammation or siderosis is present.
Even with devastating ocular injury, reconstruction and rehabilitation should be attempted prior to enucleation.
In treating IOFB complicated by traumatic optic neuropathy, there is no clear additional benefit to surgical decompression over steroids.
Combined intraocular and sub-Tenon's capsule triamcinolone acetonide is not a recommended adjunct for reducing proliferative vitreoretinopathy or improved outcomes in open globe repair.
Administer tetanus prophylaxis, if needed.
In most, if not all situations, patients should be referred urgently to ophthalmology.
Typically, patients are hospitalized following the repair of a ruptured globe and removal of a foreign body.
If foreign body is not removed, baseline electroretinogram to monitor retinal toxicity is recommended.
The rate of blindness (visual acuity <20/200) is 25% in patients with IOFB injury. B
The amount of damage from and location of initial injury, along with type of IOFB, are the most important prognostic factors. C
Initial visual acuity is important but not decisive in forecasting the final outcome. C
IOFB size >4.0 mm and comorbid corneal injury are associated with poorer final visual acuity. C
The ocular trauma score (OTS) is helpful in visual prognosis of open globe injuries. B
Sixty percent of injured eyes show improvement after treatment. C
A rural setting of the injury increases the risk of secondary endophthalmitis. C

Injury protection, initial visual acuity, and presence of retinal detachment are significant independent risk factors affecting final visual acuity for patients with ocular trauma from lawn mower accidents. C

Older, more severely injured, Medicare-insured, and White patients have a higher odds of placement in an advanced care facility (ACF) after treatment than younger, less injured, otherwise insured, and Black and Hispanic patients in the setting of firearms-associated ocular injuries. C
